title: Trump: 5/22: The Takeout with Major Garrett
description_short: Trump: 5/22: The Takeout with Major Garrett
description_medium: 5/22: The Takeout with Major Garrett. Tulsi Gabbard resigns as national intelligence director; President Trump defends "anti-weaponization" fund despite GOP backlash. This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, legal development, documented relationship, or policy consequence linked directly or indirectly to Trump. The downstream effects include institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: In the May 22, 2026 edition of The Takeout, Major Garrett opened with Tulsi Gabbard’s departure as director of national intelligence. Gabbard said she resigned after her husband received a cancer diagnosis, while reports that the White House forced her out circulated soon afterward. The episode revisited her Senate testimony: she had not endorsed the Iran war and had contradicted President Trump’s claim that Iran had renewed its nuclear ambitions after U.S. and Israeli strikes in 2025. The program also examined Trump’s defense of a Justice Department “anti-weaponization” fund despite resistance from Senate Republicans. Garrett said the fund was allotted $1.8 billion and named Michael Cohen and former Trump campaign adviser Michael Caputo as applicants. Cohen told the program he viewed his application as a test of whether the fund would be administered neutrally, given Trump’s public hostility toward him. The segment reported competing claims and applicants’ arguments; it did not establish that either man had received compensation.
topic_tags: Office of the Director of National Intelligence

title: Trump: ‘The door to the future of Gaza is still closed’: Trump’s reconstruction promises stall
description_short: Trump: ‘The door to the future of Gaza is still closed’: Trump’s reconstruction promises stall
description_medium: ‘The door to the future of Gaza is still closed’: Trump’s reconstruction promises stall. Diplomatic impasse and lack of progress on the ground has left countries that pledged funds to Board of Peace reluctant to pay This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, legal development, documented relationship, or policy consequence linked directly or indirectly to Trump. The downstream effects include institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: Seven months after Donald Trump brokered a Gaza ceasefire, reconstruction had not begun and the Board of Peace was struggling to turn pledges into funds. Nine countries pledged $7 billion at the board’s inaugural meeting, but the Guardian reported that only the United Arab Emirates and Morocco had sent contributions; it also reported $23 million for board operations and $100 million for a planned Palestinian police force. Trump separately pledged $10 billion in U.S. funding, which had not been disbursed and had not formally been requested. The board’s May 15 submission to the U.N. Security Council blamed Hamas’s refusal to disarm and relinquish control as the principal obstacle. Other people familiar with the board cited stalled diplomacy and lack of progress as reasons donors were holding back. A senior board official disputed that it faced an urgent funding problem, and accounts differed over whether Bahrain had transferred money. The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza remained in Egypt, while Israel continued to control much of the territory. The report describes a gap between announced commitments and work on the ground; it does not establish that all pledged amounts were contractually due.
topic_tags: National Committee for the Administration of Gaza

title: Trump: Why more US women are moving abroad: ‘It’s because of Trump, right? Yes and no’
description_short: Trump: Why more US women are moving abroad: ‘It’s because of Trump, right? Yes and no’
description_medium: Why more US women are moving abroad: ‘It’s because of Trump, right? Yes and no’. As many as 40% of young women say they want to migrate, citing better work life balance to Trump’s politics This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, legal development, documented relationship, or policy consequence linked directly or indirectly to Trump. The downstream effects include institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: The Guardian reported that a Gallup poll of 1,000 people found 40% of U.S. women ages 15 to 44 said they would move abroad permanently if they had the chance. The article described that as a fourfold increase from earlier versions of the question beginning in 2014; the share among young men remained around 19%. It also interviewed five women who had moved to Latin America or Europe and another planning to leave. They described several reasons, including gun violence, reproductive-rights concerns after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, work-life balance, and political turbulence. One interviewee said the 2024 election and Trump’s return confirmed an existing decision to move, while others emphasized safety, community, or practical lifestyle priorities. Expatsi co-founder Jen Barnett said politics had become the leading reason clients gave after Trump’s reelection, though the article does not treat the poll as proof that his policies alone caused migration plans. The figure measures stated interest, not completed moves; the report also notes that living abroad brings visa, salary, language, and family trade-offs.

title: Qatar Gifts Trump 400 Million Luxury Jet Raising Foreign Emoluments Clause Concerns
description_short: Qatar Gifts Trump 400 Million Luxury Jet Raising Foreign Emoluments Clause Concerns
description_medium: In May 2025, reports emerged that Qatar was gifting Trump a 400 million dollar Boeing 747 luxury aircraft for use as Air Force One. Legal experts immediately flagged violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause, which requires congressional approval for gifts from foreign governments to U.S. officials. The deal coincided with major U.S.-Qatar diplomatic activity and Qatar 2 billion dollar investment in the Trump stablecoin.
description_long: In May 2025, President Trump said the U.S. government was poised to accept a Boeing 747 from Qatar valued at nearly $400 million, which he said would replace the aging Air Force One aircraft. PBS NewsHour discussed the proposal with Kathleen Clark, a government-ethics expert, after the announcement raised legal, ethical, and national-security concerns. The reported plan placed the aircraft with the U.S. government rather than describing a private transfer to Trump, but the supplied report does not establish the final terms, whether the transfer was completed, or who would own and maintain the plane after Trump left office. Those details matter to evaluating the constitutional concern raised in coverage. The record’s additional claim that Qatar invested $2 billion in Trump’s stablecoin is not supported by the linked PBS segment. Without primary documentation for the transfer and any investment, the two claims should not be presented as a connected transaction.
